title: The slide
teaches: Mono, legato, glide and retrigger: notes that slide into each other

parts.title: From one note to the next

blocks.text: **The sound.** A singer moving from one note to another doesn't jump. The voice slides, quickly, through the pitches in between, and so does a violin or a trombone. A keyboard can't: each key is its own fixed pitch. Here is a slow line played as a keyboard plays it, then with every jump turned into a slide.

blocks.caption: A slow line, jumping and sliding

blocks.text: The slide is called **glide**, or **portamento**.[^portamento] It is one of the few controls that makes a synth sound less like a keyboard instrument and more like a voice, and it is the signature of a great many synth leads and basses.

The **Glide** knob sets how long the slide takes. At a few hundredths of a second it is barely a slide at all, more a softening of each note's start. At a fifth of a second it sounds like a deliberate swoop, and at half a second the line starts to sound drunk. Most of the useful settings are short.

blocks.caption: A slow line with no glide. Turn it up until each leap is a swoop.
blocks.task: Turn the glide up to 200 ms or more

blocks.text: Some synths take the same time for every slide, however far it goes; others move at the same speed, so a big leap takes longer than a small one.[^rate] Either way, glide is set once for a patch and left alone. On the keyboard here, play two keys an octave apart and you'll hear the slide between them.

Glide only makes sense on a synth that plays one note at a time, because a slide needs a single note to move. Such a synth is **monophonic**, or **mono**: one voice, like a singer. Hold one key and press another, and the second takes over. Let go of the second while still holding the first, and most mono synths go back to the first, the way a guitarist's finger lifted from a fret lets the lower note ring again.

This synth has been monophonic all along, which is why its keyboard has never played chords. When two keys are held, the last one pressed wins. Older synths chose differently, and a few let you set it: the lowest held key, or the highest.[^priority] It sounds like a detail, but it changes how fast runs and trills feel under the fingers. On the keyboard here, hold one key, tap another above it, and listen to the first come back.

A mono synth has one more choice to make when a new key goes down: does the new note start again? In **Retrig** mode, every key restarts the envelopes, so each note gets its own attack, however it is played. In **Legato** mode, a key pressed while another is still held carries on from where the last note was: the envelope doesn't start again, and only the pitch moves. That is how a singer slurs two notes in one breath.

Legato mode usually changes the glide too: only notes played over a held one slide, and notes played separately jump. The player then decides, note by note, which notes slide, by holding the last key down or not. In the figure, the second note is held until the third starts.

blocks.caption: Four notes as a pitch line, with their loudness below. The second is held into the third.
blocks.task: Set Legato with a glide of 80 ms or more

blocks.text: In Retrig mode every jump is a slide and every note starts again; it is smooth but samey. In Legato mode the separate notes stay crisp and only the slurred pair glides, without a new attack. That mixture of crisp and sliding notes is the sound of a great deal of electronic bass.

Now make it. This bass line has two places where a note is held into the next. The synth is in Retrig mode with no glide, so every note is a separate pluck. Make only those two slide, and let them carry on without a new pluck.

blocks.caption: A plucked bass, every note separate. Make the held notes slide.

blocks.text: Play it yourself on the keys: hold a note, press the next before you let go, and that note slides; play them apart, and it doesn't. This is the control that a step sequencer's **slide** switch flips (lesson 20), and it is most of the character of the bass lines in acid house.

blocks.caption: Five questions on the slide
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: What does the Glide knob set?
choices: How long the pitch takes to slide from one note to the next
items.why: Glide, or portamento, turns each jump in pitch into a slide of the length you set.

items.ask: A mono synth: you hold C, press E, then let go of E. What do most mono synths play?
items.why: The held key takes the voice back.

items.ask: What does Legato mode do when a key is pressed while another is held?
choices: The new note doesn't restart the envelope
items.why: In legato the envelope carries on and only the pitch moves.

items.ask: In Legato mode with glide, which notes slide?
choices: Only notes played over a held one
items.why: Separate notes jump; overlapping ones slide.

items.ask: Why does glide need a monophonic synth?
choices: A slide needs a single note to move from one pitch to the next
Glide only works on low notes
Chords are always out of tune
items.why: With several notes sounding, there is no single pitch for the next note to slide from.

summary: **Glide, or portamento, slides the pitch** from one note to the next instead of jumping.
**Short glide softens, long glide swoops**: most useful settings are a few hundredths of a second.
**A monophonic synth plays one note at a time**; the last key pressed wins, and the held key comes back when the new one is lifted.
**Retrig mode restarts the envelopes** on every key.
**Legato mode carries on** when a key is pressed over a held one: no new attack, only the pitch moves.
**In Legato mode only overlapping notes glide**, so the player chooses which notes slide.
**Crisp notes with the odd slur** is the sound of a lot of electronic bass, and of a sequencer's slide switch.

portamento.title: Portamento and glissando
portamento.text: Singers and string players call the slide between two notes portamento, Italian for carrying. A glissando, from the French for sliding, usually means sweeping through the notes in between, as a harpist runs a finger down the strings or a pianist down the white keys. A trombone can do either. On synths the two words are used loosely, and glide is the commonest name on the panel.

rate.title: Time or speed
rate.text: A glide with constant time takes, say, a fifth of a second whatever the interval, so a leap of an octave moves faster than a step of a semitone. A glide with constant rate moves at a set number of semitones per second, so the octave takes twelve times as long as the semitone. Some synths glide the first way, because a capacitor charging through a resistor takes the same time to approach any target voltage, while others use a constant-current circuit to glide at a constant rate. A few let you choose. The synth in this course uses constant time.

priority.title: Note priority
priority.text: Which key wins when several are held is called note priority. Last-note priority, the commonest today, plays the newest key. Low-note priority plays the lowest held key, which suits bass lines: hold a low note and tap higher ones for quick ornaments that fall back to it. The Minimoog worked that way. High-note priority suits leads in the same way. Some synths let you choose in a settings menu.
